#Use cases

What serviceman is for, told as the situations it is actually used in. Each one is a config you can copy.

#Development watchers

Several bin/watch scripts at once — a webpack dev server that builds an app and then rebuilds it on every change — started, stopped and restarted from one page instead of a pile of terminals.

A watcher is a program, so it is a shell service, and a program runs where an agent is: the laptop itself here, dialled in as laptop. Give each one an address and serviceman proxies to it; give it none and serviceman only keeps it running.

{
    "listen": {"host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 3000},
    "control": {"host": "serviceman.localhost", "port": 3001},
    "remotes": [
        {"name": "laptop", "token": "0c0f…a91b"}
    ],
    "services": [
        {
            "name": "app-watch",
            "title": "app · webpack",
            "type": "shell",
            "remote": "laptop",
            "publish": {"host": "app.localhost", "port": 8080},
            "command": "npm run watch",
            "cwd": "/home/user/app",
            "policy": {"start": "always", "restart": "always"}
        },
        {
            "name": "admin-watch",
            "title": "admin · webpack",
            "type": "shell",
            "remote": "laptop",
            "publish": {"host": "admin.localhost", "port": 8081},
            "command": "npm run watch",
            "cwd": "/home/user/admin",
            "policy": {"start": "always", "restart": "always"}
        },
        {
            "name": "css-watch",
            "title": "css · sass",
            "type": "shell",
            "remote": "laptop",
            "command": "npx sass --watch src:public/css",
            "cwd": "/home/user/app",
            "policy": {"start": "always", "restart": "always"}
        }
    ]
}

serviceman-agent --url http://127.0.0.1:3001 --token 0c0f…a91b

Then http://app.localhost:3000 and http://admin.localhost:3000 are the two apps, the sass watcher answers nowhere and only runs, and the control page on http://serviceman.localhost:3001 has all three.

"start": "always" is required here, not a preference. A watcher gets no HTTP traffic while you edit, so a service left on_demand would be put to sleep in the middle of your work. An always-on service is never reaped, whatever stop_after_idle says.

"restart": "always" brings a watcher back when it dies on a bad build — after 1s, then 2s, doubling to 30s, and the count resets once it has stayed up for half a minute. on_failure (the default) leaves a clean exit alone; never leaves everything alone.

What the page gives you

Want Where
The build output Not on the page yet: Logs is a place kept for it. The waiting page shows the last lines while a watcher comes up.
Kill a stuck watcher Stop. The whole process group goes, so npm run watch takes webpack with it.
Bring it back Start.
Why it died, and when The log: program_end service=app-watch how="code 1", then program_restart_wait.
All of them at a glance Services: green while they run, and the state changes as they fall over and come back.

Restart is missing. The page has Start and Stop; restarting a watcher — the thing you do most — is two clicks today, with a wait between them. A POST /api/v1/services/<name>/restart and a third button belong here.

#Catching a watcher that hangs

serviceman knows when a program exits — the agent holds the child and says so, serviceman writes program_end and lets the restart policy decide. What neither can see from outside is a program that is still running and has stopped working: the watcher that holds its port and never rebuilds again.

For that, put watchdog from @vbarbarosh/node-helpers between serviceman and the program:

{
    "name": "app-watch",
    "type": "shell",
    "publish": {"host": "app.localhost", "port": 8080},
    "command": "npx watchdog npm run watch",
    "cwd": "/home/user/app",
    "policy": {"start": "always", "restart": "always"}
}

watchdog opens a unix socket, puts WATCHDOG_SOCKET and WATCHDOG_INTERVAL in the child's environment, and waits for the child to knock on it. A ping is any connection that ends cleanly — ping_socket(process.env.WATCHDOG_SOCKET) from the same package, or a connect and a close from anything else. No ping within the interval and watchdog kills the whole process group and exits 124.

serviceman then sees what it always sees — a program that stopped, with a code:

[program_end] service=app-watch how="code 124"
[program_restart_wait] service=app-watch in_ms=1000 restart=1

So a hang becomes a restart, with no new machinery on either side. Two things to know before reaching for it: the program has to ping, so it works for code you own and not for a third-party binary; and the ping proves only that the loop doing the pinging is alive, so ping from the place that does the work, not from a timer beside it.

For a service that serves HTTP there is a cheaper answer — asking it for a page — which is what serviceman already does before it calls a service ready. Watching for that after the start, on a clock, is not built yet.

Two smaller things worth knowing

  • command runs through /bin/sh -c, so pipes, && and environment expansion work. Use argv instead when you want no shell.
  • serviceman stops the programs it started when it stops itself, through the agent. Containers outlive it and are adopted again; a program cannot be, so it is stopped rather than left orphaned.
